summary:
**Conversation overview**

This conversation is a direct continuation of an ongoing long-form computational audit project called "The Method 1.6," a multi-volume technical work. The person is acting as project manager (referred to as "M" in the project's internal documents), overseeing Claude's systematic Phase R2 review of the main volume and associated compendia. The session began with Claude executing a gated startup protocol from HANDOFF-21, fetching two large bundle files from Google Drive (BUILD90 main and BUILD96 compendia), verifying byte counts, md5 hashes, line counts, and member files against stated expectations, then running a suite of Python instruments to confirm all prior figures reproduced exactly before proceeding.

The substantive work this chat covered four reading segments: main Chapter 10 ("The void," L2021–2074), Chapter 11 ("The single expression," L2075–2303), and two subsegments of Chapter 12 (§12.1–12.5 and §12.6–12.7). For each segment Claude wrote a dedicated Python instrument (r2-ch10.py through r2-ch12b.py), re-measured every general claim on all 475,800 unordered pairs or all 976 cells as appropriate, produced a READ file documenting deviations and verified items, and wrote a CENSUS-CLOSURES file closing any open census rows. A guarded build (BUILD97) was then assembled by appending W-107 to the Working Register and adding twelve new member files; a reverse-recovery check confirmed BUILD97 restores BUILD96's md5. HANDOFF-22 was produced for the next session. The person briefly questioned whether the chat had duplicated prior work upon seeing familiar file names in the output, then withdrew the question once the distinction between carried members and new members was clarified. At close the person asked for an overall audit score, which Claude answered from measured data in the banked READ files rather than from memory.

Key findings carried forward to R3: several "iff," "exactly," and "every" claims in Chapters 10–12 are false when tested on the full lattice rather than printed samples; four printed measurements lack Register entries or recoverable populations; a pointer in Chapter 11 references its own section rather than the correct §17.4; and the "single expression" omits the cap conditions needed to select exactly 976 cells. All computed numerical values in these chapters reproduced correctly. The project disciplines established in prior chats remain in force: measure from files, never recite; label MEASURED/INFERRED/record-carried; no corrections or Register entries until the review closes; handoff at 90–95% context on a closed segment.

**Tool knowledge**

Google Drive file retrieval follows a two-step pattern that proved reliable throughout this project: search using `title contains 'BUILD97_compendia' or title contains 'BUILD90_main'` with `pageSize 5` and `excludeContentSnippets True`, then decode the spilled result with `base64.b64decode(json.loads(json.load(open(p))[0]['text'])['content'], validate=True)` — the content arrives as a base64 string nested inside a JSON object inside the tool-result JSON, and `validate=True` catches truncation. The person's key Drive folder for uploads is Materials (`1XX_5f3PZB6tjRtiZ2GIgd8Tt7i_4GgkY`). Bundle member extraction uses `re.compile(r'^<<<FILE: (.+?)>>>\n(.*?)<<<END FILE: \1>>>', re.S|re.M)` applied to the decoded text; removing `__pycache__` before any member census is a standing requirement. The reverse-recovery guard (strip new members and the WR delta, check the resulting md5 matches the prior build) is the required correctness check before any build is presented.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319

# READ-ch9 — Phase R2, main volume Chapter 9 "The arithmetic encoding" (chat 70)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L1936–L2020 (85 lines), read in full against (i) each cited section and Register entry, (ii) the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…), (iii) the chapter instrument r2-ch9.py (beside tower-2.py) and r2-tools.py. Rulings applied as in READ-ch7. Census rows in range: none; CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch9.tsv is the header alone.

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**9-01 · L2019 (§9.3) — a stated biconditional that is false in general.** PRINTED: `μ_Λ = μ_arith **iff** the interval is a void-free unit hypercube. Exact — 60 void-free pairs all agree, 56 void-bearing pairs all disagree, no mixed case.` MEASURED (r2-ch9.py, all 115,162 comparable pairs of Λ₈; μ_Λ by the closed form of L2015, itself verified against the recursive definition on 300 of 300 sampled pairs; μ_arith = the number-theoretic Möbius function of N(y)/N(x)): void-free unit hypercubes 18,103 — all agree; void-bearing unit hypercubes 17,104 — all disagree; **non-unit intervals (some Δᵢ ≥ 2) 79,955 — all agree, both functions being 0** (13,501 void-free, 66,454 void-bearing). Agreement therefore holds on 98,058 of 115,162 comparable pairs, not only on void-free unit hypercubes. READING: the 116 tested pairs were evidently all unit hypercubes, and the biconditional was stated for the whole lattice. True statement: *restricted to unit-hypercube intervals*, μ_Λ = μ_arith iff the interval is void-free; on every non-unit interval both vanish. Defect, subject-matter (an "Exact" theorem overgeneralised from its sample). For R3: restate with the restriction; a Register correction entry (both states kept).

**9-02 · L1996–2002 (§9.2 "Five equivalent forms") with L1994 and the Figure 9.1 caption L2009.** PRINTED: form 1 `|[x∧y, x∨y]| — interval count`; L1994 `The measure counts *cells*, and a cell is occupied`; L2009 `d(x,y) counts cells in the interval between two points`; `verified 500/500 and 2,000/2,000`. MEASURED (r2-ch9.py, 2,000 random pairs): forms 2, 3, 4, 5 agree 2,000/2,000; form 1 read as the number of **cells of Λ** in [x∧y, x∨y] agrees with form 2 on 580 of 2,000; over all 475,800 pairs the box [x∧y, x∨y] contains a non-cell for **340,929 (71.7 %)** and is void-free for 134,871 (28.3 %). READING: the five forms are equivalent only when the interval is taken in the divisor lattice (the box, every point of which is a divisor of lcm/gcd) — which is the encoding's own lattice (L1949) — and not in Λ, where the interval usually has voids (as §9.3 itself says at L2019). "Counts cells" is false under the natural reading for 71.7 % of pairs. Defect, subject-matter (definition stated loosely at its home). For R3: say "counts the points of the box [x∧y, x∨y] — the divisors of lcm/gcd — of which Λ's cells are a subset".

**9-03 · L1965 and L1982–1983.** PRINTED: `the orders are partial and share 0.3%`; `the 0.3% overlap`. SOURCE: 0.3 % has 7 other sites (3 in main); its definition is not given in this chapter. MEASURED here: comparable pairs are 24.2 % of all pairs (115,162 of 475,800), so 0.3 % is not comparability. Record-carried to the site that defines it (Ch. 18/27 region — to be read in its chapter); not closed here.

**9-04 · L1943–1947, L1970–1974, L1998–2002 (layout).** Space-aligned column dumps and four-space display lines (L1939, L1949, L1959, L1963, L2015) render as code blocks. MEASURED (r2-tools.py layout). Production.

## B. Verified (all MEASURED unless marked)

- L1939–1947 N(x) = ∏pᵢ^{xᵢ}: x ≤ y ⇔ N(x) | N(y), join = lcm, meet = gcd, rank Σxᵢ = Ω(N): 0 violations on all 976 cells and all 475,800 pairs.
- L1949 Λ is a sublattice of the divisor lattice of one integer (N(top)): INFERRED, immediate.
- L1952 rank = Ω(N) on all 976 cells: true.
- L1954 ω(N(x)) ≤ 8, tight at (2,1,3,3,2,1,3,3): that cell is in Λ, ω = 8 there (and at 99 other cells); ω can exceed dim = 7: true (8 > 7).
- L1959, L1971 d = ∏(|Δᵢ|+1) = τ(lcm/gcd): forms 2–5 agree on 2,000/2,000 (see 9-02 for form 1).
- L1992 d(x,x) = 1: true.
- L2003–2004 symmetric; d ≥ 1 with equality iff x = y; multiplicative triangle inequality 4,000 of 4,000: 0 violations on 4,000 fresh triples. log d = Σ log(|Δᵢ|+1) is a metric (sum of per-axis concave metrics) — INFERRED; "ordinary ℓ¹" is loose (ℓ¹ sum of log-distorted axes, as L2005 itself says); balls hyperbolic with boundary (1+Δ₁)(1+Δ₂) = D, steps log 2 and log(11/10): INFERRED, immediate.
- L2015 Möbius closed form (Rota, Λ ≅ J(P), |P| = 17): = recursive definition on 300 of 300 sampled comparable pairs; values in {−1, 0, +1} on all 115,162.
- L2019 "60 void-free pairs all agree, 56 void-bearing pairs all disagree": consistent with the measured behaviour on unit hypercubes (see 9-01 for the general statement). "Decidable in seven comparisons": the box [x∧y, x∨y] lies in Λ iff each of the seven constraints holds at its worst corner (bounded coordinate at the top, bounding coordinate at the bottom) — agrees with brute force on 3,000 pairs.
- L1972–1974 middle and third rows (17 % of 264 inputs single-valued, worst spread 12, range [3, 23]; w priced at V = 4ν/3): §12.11.0.12 (L2999) and §22.1 (L5943) — record-carried to Chapters 12 and 22. L1977 §27 "proves the three measures are one quantity" — record-carried to Ch. 27.
- L1980–1982 Theorem 18.2 (4 other main sites, L5344 …), §18.6 (L5303), §25.6.3 (L7039), §14.3 (L3719), §18.4.1 (L4999), Register 438 (R L1627): all resolve; claims record-carried to their chapters.
- Figure 9.1 placed at L2007.

## C. Incidental

- Void-free boxes are 28.3 % of all pairs and 27.4 % of comparable pairs (31,604 of 115,162); the figure may be useful to whoever restates 9-01 and 9-02.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"== MC 1660-1668
> **Prior art: the difference between a box count and the cells it actually contains is what Moebius inversion would compute. Rota (1964).**

### The void-free fraction

**The seven constraints are positively dependent over pairs of cells, and the dependence runs only along the constraint tree — proved, with the factor derived. For a pair (x,y) of Λ-cells the box [x∧y, x∨y] lies inside Λ iff each constraint xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) holds throughout it, which by monotonicity of φ is the single comparison hiᵢ ≤ φ(loⱼ) (`M §10.3`). Each comparison is a NARROWNESS condition on the coordinates it touches: at zero width in the shared coordinate it holds with probability 1, and its probability falls monotonically with that width (q ≤ k: 1.000, 0.599, 0.319 at widths 0, 1, 2). Two constraints that share a coordinate are therefore two decreasing functions of one width variable, and Chebyshev's sum inequality gives P(both) ≥ P(one)·P(other) — the dependence is positive, and it is positive for this reason and no other. Conditioned on the shared coordinate's interval (lo, hi) the two are independent: the lift P(both | interval)/(P(one | interval)·P(other | interval)) is 1.0000 in every stratum for all five shared-coordinate pairs, so all dependence flows through shared coordinates and nowhere else; constraint pairs sharing no coordinate measure lifts 0.9999–1.0101. Because the constraint graph is a tree (the constraint tree (§8.5)), the joint probability factorises along it by the chain rule, and the factor above independence is exactly the product of the six edge lifts in tree order: at caps (3,3,1,3,1), exhaustively over all 475,80

*pairs (x,y) of Λ-cells; box [x∧y, x∨y] in the ambient product of chains; containment tested as hiᵢ ≤ φ(loⱼ) per constraint; base-cap instance exhaustive at (n,e,ℓ,k,f) = (3,3,1,3,1); the 776M-pair figures at their original cap family, which the record does not name*

Proved — M §10.2, §10.3; Rota 1964; Lauritzen 1996.

== REG around 2835
2831:### 775
**P.jj's COUNT WAS INFLATED BY THIRTY PAIRS THAT CANNOT FAIL, AND THE CORRECTION COSTS A CLAIM.** *Where a compilation prints the SAME level for both J components — declining to resolve an interval it cannot measure — the two channels carry identical defects.* **Such a pair is trivially consistent: it has no way to disagree, so it tests nothing.** *The check counted them as passes.* **The figure was 82 of 95 — the thirty were counted as passes, so 52+30 over 52+13+30; the honest figure is 52 of 65.**

### 776

**TWENTY-NINE SUCH J-PAIRS SIT IN THE COLLECTED LEVELS, CONCENTRATED WHERE THE COMPILATION WAS LEAST ABLE TO RESOLVE FINE STRUCTURE** — *Si II ten, Sc III nine, Si III five, Ar II's high-ℓ three, Bi III two.* **They are not errors and the levels are not wrong; the zero is the source stating that the splitting is below what it can quote.** *§2.3: an interval of exactly 0.00 at quoted precision is not cost-resolvable, and §2.6 requires the decline to be recorded rather than absorbed.*
","stderr":""}

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"### A.10 The tree factorisation of the void count
 Statement. If the constraint graph of an index is a tree, the count of lattice cells inside a coordinate box
 factorises with no inclusion–exclusion.

 **Proof.** Root the tree. Each constraint binds one coordinate to exactly one parent, so the admissibility of a value on coordinate *i* depends only on the value at its parent. The count over the box is therefore a nested sum in which each leaf contributes an independent factor:

    |box ∩ Λ| = Σ_{internal} ∏_{leaves} #{admissible values given the parent}

 A tree has no cycles, so no configuration is counted twice and no correction term arises. ∎

 **For Λ**, with leaves 2*S* and *g*:

    #{g}  = max(0, min(hi₆, q, 2(2f+1)) − lo₆ + 1)

input.file_text:
# r2-ch10.py — Phase R2 instrument for main Chapter 10 "The void" (chat 71). Requires tower-2.py beside it.
# Every general claim is measured on ALL 475,800 unordered pairs of Λ8 cells, not on the printed samples.
import numpy as np, importlib.util, itertools, math
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('tower','tower-2.py'); tw=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(tw)
X=np.array(tw.L8(),dtype=np.int16); N=len(X); names='n l k q e f g S'.split()
print('|Λ8| =',N)
I,J=np.triu_indices(N,1); P=len(I); lo=np.minimum(X[I],X[J]).astype(np.int16); hi=np.maximum(X[I],X[J]).astype(np.int16)
box=np.prod((hi-lo+1).astype(np.int64),axis=1)
print('unordered pairs',P,'| Σ box points',int(box.sum()))
# --- brute-force |[x∧y, x∨y] ∩ Λ| for every pair (L2024's second term)
cnt=np.zeros(P,dtype=np.int32); ch=3000
for s in range(0,P,ch):
    L=lo[s:s+ch][:,None,:]; H=hi[s:s+ch][:,None,:]
    cnt[s:s+ch]=np.all((X[None,:,:]>=L)&(X[None,:,:]<=H),axis=2).sum(axis=1)
void=box-cnt
print('void(x,y) = ∏(|Δ|+1) − |box ∩ Λ|: void-free pairs',int((void==0).sum()),'= %.2f%%'%(100*(void==0).mean()),'| void-bearing',int((void>0).sum()),'| Σ void points',int(void.sum()))
# --- §10.3 seven comparisons hi_i ≤ φ(lo_j), constraint by constraint (bounded coordinate at the top, bounding at the bottom)
n,l,k,q,e,f,g,S=range(8)
C={'l≤n−1 (hydrogenic)': hi[:,l]<=lo[:,n]-1, 'k≤2(2l+1) (Pauli)': hi[:,k]<=4*lo[:,l]+2, 'q≤k (counting)': hi[:,q]<=lo[:,k],
   '2S≤k': hi[:,S]<=lo[:,k], 'g≤q (counting)': hi[:,g]<=lo[:,q], 'f≤e−1 (hydrogenic)': hi[:,f]<=lo[:,e]-1, 'g≤2(2f+1) (Pauli)': hi[:,g]<=4*lo[:,f]+2}
joint=np.ones(P,dtype=bool)
for c in C.values(): joint&=c
print('§10.3 iff: (all seven comparisons hold) == (void == 0) on all pairs:',bool(np.array_equal(joint,void==0)),'| disagreements',int((joint!=(void==0)).sum()))
rates={kname:float(v.mean()) for kname,v in C.items()}
for kname,v in rates.items(): print('   individual %-22s %.2f%%'%(kname,100*v))
prod=math.prod(rates.values()); jr=float(joint.mean())
print('   individual range %.2f–%.2f%% | product %.2f%% | joint %.2f%% | joint/product = %.4f'%(100*min(rates.values()),100*max(rates.values()),100*prod,100*jr,jr/prod))
# --- §10.4 closed form on all pairs: Σ over (n,l,k,q,e,f) in the box of [l≤n−1][1≤k≤2(2l+1)][q≤k][f≤e−1] · #{2S≤k} · #{g≤min(q,2(2f+1))}
def closed(with_S=True,with_listed=True):
    tot=np.zeros(P,dtype=np.int64)
    for nn,ll,kk,qq,ee,ff in itertools.product(range(1,4),range(0,2),range(1,4),range(0,4),range(1,4),range(0,2)):
        inb=(lo[:,n]<=nn)&(nn<=hi[:,n])&(lo[:,l]<=ll)&(ll<=hi[:,l])&(lo[:,k]<=kk)&(kk<=hi[:,k])&(lo[:,q]<=qq)&(qq<=hi[:,q])&(lo[:,e]<=ee)&(ee<=hi[:,e])&(lo[:,f]<=ff)&(ff<=hi[:,f])
        if not inb.any(): continue

 2313|  exchanged under ν ↦ ν⁻³.

 2316| 
 2317|     Λ is orientable. It is a cylinder.
 2318| 
 2319|  That is a *reason*, not an absence. And both alternative routes to a Möbius band close: a non-monotone quantity has **undefined** edges rather than reversing ones; a quantity independent of ν has **no** edge. There is no third option.
 2320|

 2324|  ↦ ν⁻³. The sign structure is bipartite, so no traverse can reverse orientation an odd number of times — the surface is a
 2325|  cylinder, not a Möbius band, and the reason is structural rather than an absence of evidence.
 2326| 
 2327| ### 12.2 "Over ν", not "graded by ν"
 2328|  ν grades every chain of Λ. It grades Λ itself nowhere — 24 of 70 comparable pairs have ν decreasing.
 2329| 
 2330|  **That near-miss is the structure in one sentence.** The bracket of Part V operates along chains *because that is exactly where ν is a grading.*
 2331| 
 2332|  The name follows: **the Lach Cylinder — a hydrogenic cylinder over ν, and over the transfer.** Not *graded by*. *Over.*
 2333|

 2340|  10⁻¹⁶.
 2341| 
 2342|  Λ *decomposes* ν and gains dimension; the bound lattice *recomposes* it and sheds dimension. **Two sides of one object, not two passes over it.**
 2343| 
 2344| ### 12.5 What Λ is a property of
 2345|  Λ is a property of the hydrogenic limit. δ — the quantum defect — is the entire remainder.
 2346| 
 2347|     Prediction lives only in the remainder.
 2348| 
 2349|  Which is why perfecting the index moves nothing, and why that is a theorem rather than a disappointment. Part III proves it; Part V measures what is left.
 2350|

### The surface is a cylinder

**Λ's derived quantities split into two classes — *e*, ν, *V* rising up a series and *T*, *r*, δ, spacing, *w* falling — exchanged under the map ν ↦ ν⁻³, so the sign structure is bipartite; and a bipartite sign structure can reverse orientation only an even number of times along any closed traverse, which makes the surface orientable, a cylinder and not a Möbius band. The finding is a reason, not an absence of one: verified exhaustively, zero orientation-reversing loops among all cycles of length 3 through 5, and both alternative routes to a twist close by construction — a non-monotone quantity contributes an *undefined* edge rather than a reversing one, and a quantity independent of ν contributes *no* edge, leaving no third way to build a reversal. The structural guarantee is underwritten by the shape of the constraint graph itself: it is a tree — eight vertices and seven edges, connected and acyclic, measured in every other shape the lattice contains (§12.9) — so §12.1's orientability follows from the construction and not from a search that merely failed to find a counterexample. The cylinder is a cylinder over the transfer coordinate *q*, the base of the fibration whose fibres the two-body separation (§12.6.1) computes.**

*the two derived-quantity classes of §12.1 under ν ↦ ν⁻³; orientability certified exhaustively over cycles of length 3–5 and structurally from the tree constraint graph; at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1).*

Proved — M §12.1; König 1936; Harary 1953; Listing 1861; Möbius 1865; Freuder 1982.

 **And the widths fall fast** — at ν = 40 from 0.362 cm⁻¹ at order 1 to **8.9 × 10⁻⁶ at order 5.**

# r2-ch12a: §12.1's bipartite sign structure — every cycle of length 3–5 on the eight derived quantities has an even number of reversing (cross-class) edges
import itertools
asc=['e','nu','V']; desc=['T','r','delta','spacing','w']; Q=asc+desc; cls={q:(0 if q in asc else 1) for q in Q}
rev=lambda a,b: cls[a]!=cls[b]
tot=bad=0
for L in (3,4,5):
    seen=set()
    for cyc in itertools.permutations(Q,L):
        if cyc[0]!=min(cyc): continue
        key=(cyc[0],)+min(cyc[1:],cyc[1:][::-1]); 
        if key in seen: continue
        seen.add(key); tot+=1
        if sum(rev(cyc[i],cyc[(i+1)%L]) for i in range(L))%2: bad+=1
print('cycles of length 3–5 on the complete graph of the 8 quantities: %d; with an odd number of reversing edges: %d'%(tot,bad))
EOF

 2358|

 2360|  As a bare product it fails: |A| × |B| × |q| = 2,244 against 976. The two ends are coupled twice over — q
 2361|  ≤ k ties the transfer to the parent, g ≤ q ties the target's occupancy to the transfer.
 2362|
